rationale: A wins because it turns thin company-generated news into three clean, beat-specific stories without dressing them in borrowed mythology. Its strongest line, "Liquid Death opens a store that sells almost no water," is a sharp retail-strategy provocation, even if it needs proof. B has usable bones, but "a brand that grew through cans-on-shelves and viral video" and "brand built on shock marketing" are facts smuggled in from outside the update; that is how decent angles get reporter-shaped and fact-checker-killed.
gaps_in_A: "Liquid Death opens a store that sells almost no water" overstates the update. The facts say merch, limited-edition canned water, and events; they do not prove the store sells almost no water.

"the prevailing belief is that packaged single-serve water is the category sustainability certification exists to discourage" is a smart tension, but it needs support. As written, it imports a category assumption the update does not establish.
"That's a live argument in this beat" is plausible but unproven. A should either cite the need for current standards coverage or soften it as a reporting question.
gaps_in_B: "DTC-native," "viral video," "anti-marketing," and "media brand to retail operator" are not in the update. They may be true in the real world, but this exercise gave you facts, not a permission slip to free-associate.

"Liquid Death opens its first permanent store as it converts to a B Corp" is sloppy. The company became certified this quarter; it did not necessarily "convert," and the store opening and certification are not one clean dated moment.

"brand built on shock marketing" and "irreverent, death-themed marketing" make the B Corp angle depend on brand lore the update never supplied. The better story is certification mechanics, not vibes about the skull on the can.
"but won't show net profit" overstates "has not disclosed net profit." Non-disclosure is a fact; refusal is a posture. Don't make the company more evasive than the record supports.
